name: Downstream, Upstream, Still-Water Speed, and Current
description: Build the core river-speed model and move confidently between downstream, upstream, still-water, and current speeds.
script_scope: Teach downstream as boat speed in still water plus current, and upstream as boat speed in still water minus current. Use a moving-belt mental model so the signs make sense. Cover recovering still-water speed as half the sum of downstream and upstream speeds and current speed as half their difference, deriving observed speeds from distance and time, finding a missing upstream or downstream speed from the other quantities, and checking that upstream is slower than downstream. Include source-shaped questions where downstream and upstream speeds are hidden inside different distances and times.

name: Time and Distance Ratios in a Current
description: Use same-distance and same-time shortcuts to turn rowing times and distance ratios into speed ratios.
script_scope: Teach that for the same distance, rowing time is inversely proportional to effective speed, while for the same time, distance is proportional to effective speed. Convert downstream:upstream speed ratios into still-water:current ratios using half-sum and half-difference. Cover ratios of still-water speed to current, upstream/downstream time ratios, fixed-current problems where the two travel times determine the boat speed, equal-time unequal-distance questions, and source patterns such as a boat taking 8 hours upstream and 6 hours downstream or taking a multiple of the time to return.

name: Round Trips, Total Time, and Average Speed
description: Handle out-and-back journeys by adding the two travel times and using total distance over total time for the whole trip.
script_scope: Teach an upstream-downstream round trip as two equal-distance legs with different effective speeds. Cover finding the one-way distance from total time, finding total time from a known distance, equal-distance average speed using total distance divided by total time, comparing a boat round trip with a road traveller, partial returns such as coming back to a midpoint, and reverse problems where total round-trip time plus current speed determines still-water speed. Include the chapter pattern where a boat of known still-water speed travels a fixed distance downstream and back in a given total time, leading to a simple quadratic that factors cleanly.

name: Reverse Boat-and-Current Equations
description: Turn time differences, same-time distances, and known journey times into equations for the unknown boat or current speed.
script_scope: Teach learners to choose one unknown, express downstream and upstream speeds as u+v and u−v, and build an equation from time = distance/speed. Cover equal-distance time differences, upstream time being a multiple of downstream time, same-time unequal distances, deriving current from separate downstream/upstream journeys, solving still-water speed from a round-trip total with known current, and newer source patterns where a speed ratio or measured upstream rate is used to predict another distance or travel time.

name: Mixed Upstream–Downstream Systems
description: Solve two mixed-journey conditions to recover upstream and downstream rates, then convert them to boat and current speeds.
script_scope: Teach the chapter’s two-equation pattern where one journey mixes upstream and downstream distances and a second journey gives another mix. Introduce p = 1/(upstream speed) and q = 1/(downstream speed) when that turns reciprocal equations into a simple linear system. Cover swapped-distance systems, extracting still-water/current speeds after solving the two effective rates, equidistant three-town river problems, and two-boat problems that share the same current. Keep algebra readable and verify recovered rates by replaying one original trip.

name: Swimming Across a Flowing River
description: Separate crossing speed from sideways current and solve the chapter’s straight-across swimming problems.
script_scope: Teach the chapter’s two crossing setups. First, when a swimmer heads across the width and is allowed to be carried sideways, crossing time depends on river width and swimming speed in still water; the current changes the landing point, not the across-time. Second, when the swimmer must land directly opposite, part of the swimming speed must cancel the current; use the right-triangle relation behind the chapter formula to find current speed or crossing time. Cover width recovery, sideways drift, the source 100-m river with 4-minute no-current and 5-minute flowing-water times, and feasibility checks that still-water swimming speed must exceed current speed for a directly-opposite landing.

name: Linked and Advanced Boat Journeys
description: Combine the core river-speed ideas in multi-stage, multi-town, and two-boat exam problems.
script_scope: Use integrated source-shaped applications rather than a new formula. Cover comparing a cyclist’s round trip with a boat’s, downstream travel followed by a partial upstream return, three equidistant towns on one river, two boats sharing the same current, speed-ratio questions that feed a later distance calculation, the chapter pattern where doubling the rowing rate changes the upstream/downstream time gap, same-time downstream/upstream distance conditions, and a capstone that combines two mixed journey facts. Learners should identify the effective speed on each leg before calculating anything.

name: Data Sufficiency for Boats and Streams
description: Judge whether river-speed statements determine a unique answer without doing unnecessary calculation.
script_scope: Teach data sufficiency using the chapter’s dedicated exercise. Distinguish a ratio from an actual numerical scale, recognise when upstream/downstream times share an unknown distance and still fail to determine the speed, identify pairs of statements that together determine effective rates, and spot redundant statements. Include two-statement and three-statement patterns, “either statement alone”, “both together necessary”, “even together insufficient”, and “any two of three” outcomes. Keep the focus on uniqueness of the requested quantity rather than on fully solving every question.
